content: A two-dimensional gas is defined as a collection of N objects that are restricted to move within a planar or other two-dimensional space while existing in a gaseous state. These objects can include ideal gas elements, such as rigid disks undergoing elastic collisions, elementary particles, or any physical entities that adhere to the laws of motion. The concept of a two-dimensional gas is employed either because the phenomenon under investigation inherently occurs in two dimensions (e.g., certain surface molecular phenomena) or because the two-dimensional representation of the problem is more mathematically manageable compared to its three-dimensional counterpart. Although physicists have studied simple two-body interactions on a plane for centuries, the study of a two-dimensional gas involving many bodies in motion became a focus of research in the 20th century. This research has contributed to advancements in understanding gas thermodynamics, specific solid-state problems, and various aspects of quantum mechanics. In the early 1960s, research at Princeton University explored whether the Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics and other thermodynamic laws could be derived from Newtonian mechanics applied to multi-body systems, rather than relying on traditional statistical mechanics methods. While this question is challenging to address in three-dimensional systems, it behaves differently in two-dimensional space. Specifically, an ideal two-dimensional gas was analyzed in terms of its relaxation time to equilibrium velocity distribution, starting from various arbitrary initial conditions. The relaxation times were found to be remarkably fast, on the order of the mean free time. In 1996, a computational approach was applied to the classical mechanics problem of non-equilibrium heat flow within a two-dimensional gas. The simulations demonstrated that for systems with more than 1500 particles, the results closely matched those of continuous systems, such as two-dimensional gas dynamics. Early investigations also examined the behavior of a two-dimensional electron gas, particularly in relation to cyclotron resonance and the de Haas-van Alphen effect. It was shown that, for a two-dimensional gas, the period of de Haas-van Alphen oscillations is independent of short-range electron interactions. In 1991, theoretical work provided proof that a Bose gas could exist in two dimensions. The same study proposed experimental methods to verify this hypothesis. Experimental research using a molecular gas was conducted by Stranick, who employed an ultra-high vacuum scanning microscope to image a two-dimensional benzene gas layer in contact with a planar solid interface at 77 kelvins. The researchers observed benzene molecules moving freely as a two-dimensional gas on the surface of Cu(III), to which a planar monomolecular film of solid benzene adhered. This allowed the scientists to observe the equilibrium of the gas in contact with its solid state, including transient migration and phase transitions of individual benzene molecules. The study of two-dimensional gases opens numerous avenues for future research in theoretical physics. These include investigations into melting phenomena at planar surfaces, thin film phenomena such as chemical vapor deposition, and surface excitations of solids.
